The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established.

The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. The one direct measurement read (Henry et al., 1998) gave 8 normally hydrated healthy men aged 22 to 32 a single capsule of MDMA (47.5 mg of the hydrochloride, equal to 40 mg of MDMA base) with 200 mL of water (study conditions): vasopressin peaked 1 to 2 hours later, from a range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L before the dose to 2.46 to 9.16 pmol/L at 2 hours (one-tailed p = 0.006), and blood sodium fell by 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of the 8 and rose by 1 mmol/L in the eighth (one-tailed p = 0.025), with every 2-hour value between 140 and 142 mmol/L, above the 130 mmol/L used for low sodium in the case series (editors' comparison). Its only comparison was 3 of the same men on a later, untreated occasion, when vasopressin fell slightly; the two kinds of occasion were not compared statistically, so the rise cannot be cleanly separated from other changes during the day, and the study tested no extra drinking, measured no urine, studied no illness and included no women. A placebo-controlled crossover study of 32 healthy volunteers given 125 mg (study condition; Hysek et al., 2014) found no significant change in copeptin, the C-terminal part of the hormone's precursor, measured before and 1 and 2 hours after the dose (no statistic printed), and did not measure sodium.
plain
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water; that part is not proven.

The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water. In one small study, 8 healthy men given a single capsule of MDMA had a rise in the water-holding hormone 1 to 2 hours later and a small fall in blood sodium (by 1 to 3 units, not to a low level), but it had no proper comparison, and a study of 32 volunteers found no clear rise in a related marker. So that part is not proven.
magnitude
No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts. Volunteers (Henry et al., 1998; 8 healthy men, 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride, equal to 40 mg base, with 200 mL water at 10:00): vasopressin range 1.14–1.88 pmol/L before and 2.46–9.16 at 2 hours (paired t test, one-tailed p = 0.006; about 0.012 two-tailed, editors' calculation), peak between 1 and 2 hours; sodium 139–145 mmol/L before and 140–142 at 2 hours, down 1–3 in 7 of 8 and up 1 in one (one-tailed p = 0.025; about 0.05 two-tailed, editors' calculation); cortisol 331.4 (208.8–603.4) to 377.2 (268.4–583.3) nmol/L, not significant; vasopressin and MDMA not correlated (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 0.1); 3 later untreated control occasions in the same men, not compared statistically. Hysek et al. (2014; 32 healthy volunteers, 125 mg against placebo, crossover): copeptin before and 1 and 2 hours after not changed (no statistic printed; Figure 4B, editors' reading, peak change about +2 pg/mL after MDMA and about -1 after placebo).

grade.reasoning
The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts.

The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and is neither asserted nor rated: the one direct measurement read (Henry et al., 1998; card sc_henry_1998, ROBINS-I serious) is a before-and-after study of 8 men with one-tailed tests at the 2-hour point only and 3 later untreated occasions that were not compared statistically, and a placebo-controlled study of 32 volunteers found no significant change in copeptin (Hysek et al., 2014); neither tested extra drinking, measured urine or studied illness, so neither bears on the case pattern the claim describes.

evidence_add.locator: Letter, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column); figure legend (right column)
evidence_add.extracted: Research letter testing whether the low sodium seen after MDMA is a direct effect of vasopressin secretion. Eight normally hydrated healthy men aged 22 to 32 each took 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (equivalent to 40 mg MDMA base) in a capsule with 200 mL of water at 10:00 (study conditions); three of them acted as untreated controls on an occasion at least 2 weeks later (the figure legend calls this condition placebo, n = 3). Blood was taken before and 30 minutes and 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 24 hours after, for MDMA, vasopressin (radioimmunoassay), cortisol and sodium; before-and-after comparisons by repeated-measures analysis of variance or paired t test. Approved by the UK Home Office and a King's College London ethics committee. The letter describes no women, no fluid given beyond the 200 mL and no urine measurement.

evidence_add.extracted: The authors call the dose relatively small (stating, without a source, that street ecstasy frequently contains more than 100 mg), say the rise came at a time of day when vasopressin would not be expected to change, and conclude that the low-sodium illness is likely linked to MDMA's ability to stimulate vasopressin secretion, that with excessive fluid even a small dose could lead to symptoms, and that the rise is not part of a general stress response because cortisol did not change significantly. The letter tested none of these conclusions: it gave no fluid load, measured no urine and studied no illness, and its closing message about fluid intake and its statement on thirst and judgement rest on no data from the study.
